text:
The exercise is called Jammertest. Each September, Norwegian authorities create controlled interference around the Arctic island of Andoya, where companies and researchers can discover how their navigation equipment fails. ESA's October second report describes the latest campaign, which took place in September. The footage marked archive shows the earlier, twenty twenty-five tests. The new photographs show this year's work.

There are different ways to mislead a receiver. Jamming overwhelms the genuine satellite signals, so a device may lose its position altogether. Spoofing supplies false signals, making a convincing location appear somewhere else. Meaconing captures genuine signals and broadcasts them again with a misleading delay or location. 

And the stakes extend beyond the blue dot on a phone. Satellite signals also provide precise time for infrastructure. Aviation, power networks and emergency services depend on reliable positioning or timing. A controlled test lets engineers compare different receivers and antennas against the same difficult conditions, instead of waiting for a failure during an actual journey.

One part of the campaign tested Galileo's future Signal Authentication Service. On September sixteenth, receivers established their position using an encrypted test signal. That milestone was already announced in September; it did not happen on October second. Signal authentication is intended to help receivers recognise legitimate signals and reject many spoofing attempts. It does not make every receiver immune to interference, and the new service is not yet protection built into every phone.

ESA also tracked signals from the Celeste demonstration satellites under contested conditions. Those results remain preliminary. The data still need analysis before firmer conclusions. Updated monitoring-station prototypes for EGNOS underwent further tests too. 

The practical lesson is that navigation needs more than a plausible position on a screen. It needs trustworthy signals, resilient receivers and evidence from demanding tests. Jammertest brings those pieces together in a controlled field environment. The report describes progress, not a guarantee that satellite deception has been solved.
